textbookText: In the case of a falling body, assuming air resistance is negligible (so that only gravitational force is acting), mechanical energy is conserved. Statement: Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed, but it can be changed from one form to another form.
OR Physics, Grade 11 | 115
The total mechanical energy of an isolated system remains conserved.
Proof:
Fig 5.6b: Showing conservation of mechanical energy
Let us consider a body of mass m allowed to fall freely under gravity from a height h above the ground level at point A.

The body begins to fall from its zero value (uA = 0) at point A, reaches first to point B (AB =x), and finally on the ground at point C (BC= h –x). vB and vC are the velocities at the respective points B & C.
Now at point A,
P.E = mgh = mg×h = mgh
Therefore, total energy = K.E+P.E = 0+ mgh = mgh
At point B,
K.E = 𝟏mv2 = 𝟏mvB2 = 𝟏m (uA2 +2gx) =𝟏m.2gx = mgx
P.E = mgh = mg (h-x) =mgh – mgx
Therefore, total energy = K.E+P.E = mgx +mgh – mgx = mgh
At point C,
K.E = 𝟏mv2 = 𝟏mvC2 = 𝟏m (uA2 +2gh) = 𝟏m.2gh = mgh
P.E = mgh =mg×0 = 0
Therefore, total energy = K.E +P.E = mgh +0 = mgh
Physics, Grade 11 | 116

Hence, in the above three points, the total mechanical energy remains conserved. Only it is changing from P.E. to K.E. Hence the total mechanical energy remains conserved. Only it is changing from one form to another form and the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.

Do you Know? i) A body falling towards the Earth in air has frictional force due to the air resistance in addition to the conservative force such as gravitational force and hence the total mechanical energy isn’t conserved. ii) A driver accelerates his vehicle while moving up a hill. As the vehicle speeds up, the height from the ground level increases, thereby increasing the potential energy. Hence, kinetic energy decreases. To maintain kinetic energy and to speed up the vehicle, the driver accelerates his vehicle.

Fig 5.8 5.7 Conservative and Non- conservative Forces 5.7.1 Conservative force: It is the force under the action of which total mechanical energy remains conserved. Gravitational force, elastic force, magnetic force, electrostatic force, and all the field forces are examples of the conservative force. A conservative force has the following properties: i) It is independent of the path, but depends on the initial and the final position of the body.

Fig 5.9: Showing the nature of conservative force ii) Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is zero. iii) Work done by it is completely recoverable and is central in nature. iv) Conservative forces permit one to write elegant conservation laws, such as the conservation of mechanical energy. Ef = Ei Physics, Grade 11 | 118

5.7.2 Non- Conservative Force: It is the force under the action of which total mechanical energy isn’t conserved. This is because a part of the energy is dissipated in the form of sound, heat, etc. Frictional forces, tension forces, push and pull actions, applied forces, and viscous forces are examples of non-conservative forces. A non-conservative force has the following properties: i) It is path-dependent force. More work will be done on a longer path. ii) The work done by a non-conservative force around a closed path is not zero. For example, consider going from home to college and back. The work done in both the paths is against friction and differs, resulting in a non-zero value of the work done. The longer the path, the more work friction does. iii) Work done by it isn’t completely recoverable and is retarding in nature. iv) The non-conservative forces disrupt the fundamental conservation laws, such as the conservation of mechanical energy Ef < Ei Unless one adds the explicit factor for work, they do:
Ef = Ei + W One can improve the law of conservation of mechanical energy to work in real-world situations by accounting for friction:
KEf +GPEf = KEi+ GPEi +Wf, Wf→ work done by friction.
